lead: Chromatography and electrophoresis both separate the molecules of a mixture. Chromatography uses a moving mobile phase and a stationary phase; each solute divides between them differently and so travels at its own speed. Electrophoresis uses an electric field: a charged molecule feels a force qE and drifts at a speed set by its charge and friction. Clinical labs use these methods for glycated haemoglobin, drug levels, urine steroids, amino acids, serum proteins, haemoglobin variants and DNA.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for UV absorbance and the densitometer, and 3.7 for a clear serum before the run.

blocks.text: A mixture is placed at the start of a column or sheet. The mobile phase is a gas or liquid that flows and carries solutes. The stationary phase is a solid or liquid film that does not move. Each solute divides between the phases. A solute that spends more time in the stationary phase is retarded more and leaves later. Separation is by partition (dissolves in both phases) or adsorption (sticks to the solid).

In column methods (gas chromatography and HPLC) a peak is described by its retention time t<sub>R</sub>, the time from injection to the peak maximum; under fixed conditions each compound has its own t<sub>R</sub>. On a plate or a paper sheet there is no injection: the solvent rises for a fixed time, and each spot is described by its retardation factor R<sub>f</sub>. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) uses a coated plate and a rising solvent; paper chromatography uses water held in paper fibres; column chromatography packs the stationary phase in a tube.
R<sub>f</sub> = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front
blocks.where: both distances are measured from the starting line, in the same units; R<sub>f</sub> has no unit and lies between 0 and 1.

blocks.text: Gas chromatography (GC) uses a carrier gas and a heated column; a flame ionisation detector burns organic molecules and measures ion current. HPLC uses small packed particles, so liquid is pumped at high pressure; a UV detector is common, at 280 nm for proteins and at about 415 nm for haemoglobin in glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) tests. Clinical uses: glycated haemoglobin, drug levels, urine steroids, amino acids.

sections.h3: Electrophoresis: speed set by charge and friction

blocks.text: An electrophoresis tank applies an electric field E (V/m) across a buffer-soaked support. A molecule with charge q (C) feels force qE. It accelerates until friction balances that force, then drifts at speed v (m/s).

blocks.where: v is drift speed (m/s); μ is mobility (m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹); E is field strength (V/m); q is charge (C); f is the friction factor (N·s/m).

blocks.text: The sign of the charge follows buffer pH relative to the protein's isoelectric point pI. At pH 8.6 serum proteins are net negative and migrate to the anode. Mobility depends on charge, size and shape.

Paper and cellulose acetate carry serum proteins and haemoglobin variants. Agarose gel is used for DNA, negative from phosphate groups. In SDS-PAGE the detergent SDS binds to the proteins, masks their own charge and makes them all negative, so they separate by molecular weight: smaller moves faster. Isoelectric focusing uses a pH gradient; a protein stops at its pI, where net charge is zero. Capillary electrophoresis uses a narrow tube and high voltage.

Serum protein electrophoresis on cellulose acetate at pH 8.6 gives albumin, α₁, α₂, β and γ bands. Albumin is fastest and most abundant. A densitometer scans the stained strip and reports each band as a percentage of total protein.

figure.caption: Left, a TLC plate run until the solvent front is 8.0 cm up: spot A has moved 2.0 cm (R<sub>f</sub> 0.25) and spot B 5.6 cm (R<sub>f</sub> 0.70). Right, the densitometer scan of serum protein electrophoresis at pH 8.6: albumin runs furthest toward the anode and makes 60 % of the 70 g/L total, that is 42 g/L.

spec.aria: Thin-layer plate with a starting line, two spots at 2.0 and 5.6 centimetres and the solvent front at 8.0 centimetres, beside a densitometer trace with peaks for gamma 15 percent, beta 12, alpha-2 9, alpha-1 4 and a tall albumin peak of 60 percent nearest the anode.

examples.question: Serum protein electrophoresis on cellulose acetate at pH 8.6 is run on a sample with total protein 70 g/L. The densitometer reads albumin 60 %, α₁ 4 %, α₂ 9 %, β 12 % and γ 15 %. Calculate the albumin and γ-globulin concentrations in g/L.
examples.answer: Albumin is 42 g/L and γ-globulin is 10.5 g/L.
examples.check:
total = 70.0
alb_frac = 0.60
gamma_frac = 0.15
print(alb_frac * total)
print(gamma_frac * total)

examples.question: A TLC plate is run until the solvent front is 8.0 cm above the starting line. Spot A has moved 2.0 cm and spot B 5.6 cm. Find both R<sub>f</sub> values and say which compound is held more strongly by the stationary phase.
steps: R<sub>f</sub> = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front.
A moved less, so it spent more time held by the stationary phase.
examples.answer: R<sub>f</sub>(A) = 0.25 and R<sub>f</sub>(B) = 0.70; compound A is held more strongly by the stationary phase.

examples.question: A cellulose acetate strip has 200 V across a length of 10 cm. In 40 min the albumin band moves 3.0 cm toward the anode. Find the field, the drift speed and the mobility of albumin, and how far it moves in 60 min.
steps: Field E = V / length = 200 V / 0.10 m = 2000 V/m.
Drift speed v = distance / time = 0.030 m / (40 × 60 s) = 0.030 / 2400 = 1.25 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m/s.
Mobility μ = v / E = 1.25 × 10<sup>−5</sup> / 2000 = 6.25 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.
examples.answer: E = 2000 V/m, v = 1.25 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m/s, μ = 6.25 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹; in 60 min the band moves 4.5 cm.

traps: At pH 8.6 serum proteins are net negative and move to the anode; albumin is fastest, γ slowest.
Retention time belongs to column chromatography; R<sub>f</sub> belongs to plates and paper; migration distance or mobility belongs to electrophoresis.
SDS-PAGE reports molecular weight, not net charge, because SDS masks the protein's own charge.
In HPLC the small packed particles are the stationary phase; high pressure is needed for flow, not heating.
In isoelectric focusing the protein stops at pH = pI because net charge is zero, even though the field remains on.

quiz.q: Define mobile phase and stationary phase in chromatography.
quiz.a: Mobile phase flows and carries solutes; stationary phase stays fixed and retards them.

quiz.q: Why does a solute that spends more time in the stationary phase leave later?
quiz.a: A solute moves only while it is in the mobile phase. The more time it spends held in the stationary phase, the less time it moves, so it travels more slowly and its retention time is longer.

quiz.q: List the serum protein bands at pH 8.6, fastest first.
Why does SDS-PAGE separate proteins by molecular weight, not net charge?
quiz.a: SDS masks intrinsic charge and gives similar negative charge per mass; size then controls speed.

quiz.q: Total protein is 68 g/L and albumin is 55 %. Find the albumin concentration.
A protein with pI 5.0 is placed in electrophoresis at pH 8.6. Predict its charge and direction.
quiz.a: pH is above pI, so the protein is net negative; it moves to the anode.

beyond: Not for the exam. Clinical labs increasingly couple HPLC or capillary electrophoresis to mass spectrometry for drug and metabolite measurement. Capillary electrophoresis is used for haemoglobin variant screening and some HbA1c methods. SDS-PAGE with western blotting is a research and diagnostic tool for specific proteins. Search next for HPLC, capillary electrophoresis, SDS-PAGE and isoelectric focusing.
